# CHRONIC BACTERIAL PROSTATITIS

Chronic bacterial prostatitis usually presents as recurrent urinary tract infections with the same bacterial etiology. Pain, tenderness, and fever may accompany intermittent episodes of cystitis, but men are usually asymptomatic between episodes and the prostate examination may be normal. Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) often relieve pain. If the diagnosis is uncertain or if the patient's symptoms do not respond to therapy, consult urology. The presence of hematuria may be a sign of carcinoma, especially in older men, and a urology consult should be requested.

A urine culture should be performed in all patients to guide antimicrobial therapy. [Lab Menu](urine-culture)

Gram-negative rods are the most common etiologic agents, with Escherichia coli causing approximately 75 to 80 percent of episodes. Enterococcus faecalis, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Proteus mirabilis, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and other gram-negative bacilli are the next most commonly reported organisms.
Staphylococcus aureus and streptococcal species are occasional pathogens.
Chronic bacterial prostatitis is often presumptively diagnosed and empirically treated with antimicrobials when men present with chronic (eg, longer than three months) or recurrent urogenital symptoms, particularly if bacteriuria is also present. Pain, tenderness, and fever may accompany intermittent episodes of cystitis, but men are usually asymptomatic between episodes and the prostate examination may be normal. Non-steroidal anti- inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) often relieve pain. Referral to an urologist can be helpful for men with long-standing or refractory prostatic symptoms to obtain expressed prostatic fluid for diagnosis.
